catalog_quote: [p. 69] The high central vowel /ɨ/ is neutral in regard to tongue root position. It is lax but is not considered to be [-ATR], since it does not participate in the vowel harmony system (cf. section 5.1). /ɨ/ occurs in morphemes which are never stressed such as prefixes and proclitic grammatical particles: [p. 70] /mɨ-/ + /tɔ́nɔ́/ --> /mɨtɔ́nɔ́/ 'nominalizer' 'begin' 'beginning' ... It usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables: [bɨ̀lúndù] /bɨ̀lúndù/ 'grandfather' ... However, there are a few examples in which a vowel other than /ɨ/ occurs in the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. /mbɔ́lífɔ́/ 'pigeon' and /gbɛ̀gbɛ́rì/ 'throat'. ... [sec. 3. new_statements.quote: The high central vowel /ɨ/ is neutral in regard to tongue root position. [...] /ɨ/ occurs in morphemes which are never stressed such as prefixes and proclitic grammatical particles: /mɨ-/ + /tɔ́nɔ́/ --> /mɨtɔ́nɔ́/ 'nominalizer' 'begin' 'beginning' [...] It usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables: [bɨ̀lúndù] /bɨ̀lúndù/ 'grandfather' [...] [note 5:] Considering the slim evidence for treating [ɨ] as a phoneme, it is not impossible that a stress rule or a morphophonemic rule could be found to handle [ɨ] as a reduced allophone of some underlying vowel. [sec. 3:] Baka has a two-register tone system.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and rendered PDF pp. 76, 77 and 91 (printed pp. 69, 70, 84) to images; compared against the scanned file lines 399-414, 435, 1315-1319). All four quoted pieces are on the page exactly as reported (the reader's quote is a stitched excerpt with [..] marking the omissions): p. 69 bottom 'The high central vowel /ɨ/ is neutral in regard to tongue root position.. /ɨ/ occurs in morphemes which are never stressed such as prefixes and proclitic grammatical particles:'; p. 70 top the /mɨ-/ + 'begin' -> 'beginning' example, then 'It usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables: [bɨ̀lúndù] /bɨ̀lúndù/ grandfather, /màngɨ̀rɔ̀kɔ̀/ woman's…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Baka is described as a two-tone (H/L) language; Parker gives no rule for where stress falls. The only stress information is negative/impressionistic: prefixes and proclitics are never stressed, and in trisyllabic stems (presyllable + CVCV root) the antepenultimate presyllable is unstressed, implying prominence lies within the final disyllabic root, locus unspecified.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; Parker notes a few words with a full (non-ɨ) vowel in the antepenultimate syllable (/mbɔ́lífɔ́/ 'pigeon', /gbɛ̀gbɛ́rì/ 'throat') but says nothing about their stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks made in passing within the vowel description; sentence-level intonation (sec. 6) separately notes extra-high pitch on penultimate syllables in questions. No dedicated stress/accent section exists in the article.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Baka of South Sudan (Maridi area; ISO bdh, Glottolog baka1274, Central Sudanic, Bongo-Baka group) -- not the Ubangian Baka of Cameroon/Gabon (bkc). Parker's data are from Maridi (acknowledging Edward Mandeson, IRL Maridi); no dialect differentiation is made. The Tucker & Bryan 1966 stress remark is a Bongo-Bagirmi group-level statement illustrated with Bagirmi, not a Baka statement.

new_statements.quote: 2b. Stress Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI kala, snake, for instance. 3. Word Shape

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Bongo-Bagirmi group as a whole (Baka is a member): stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, always so when the second syllable has a 'semi-mute' (reduced) vowel; occasionally on the second syllable when the first has a central vowel. No Baka-specific statement and no rule for words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Stevenson's Bagirmi kala 'snake').
new_statements.identity_note: All items concern Baka of South Sudan (Maridi area), ISO bdh, Central Sudanic, Bongo-Bagirmi (Bongo-Baka) group, not the Ubangian Baka of Cameroon/Gabon. The Tucker & Bryan 1966 stress paragraph is a generalization over the whole Bongo-Bagirmi group (Bagirmi, Sara, Kresh, Bongo, Baka, etc.), with its example from Stevenson's Bagirmi manuscript; the chapter's Baka data come from Tucker's own notes and Santandrea. The Tucker 1940 archive.org copy is the 1967 Dawsons of Pall Mall reprint.

readall_conflicts: No source states a Baka-specific stress-placement rule. Parker 1985 (already in the catalog) describes a two-register H/L tone system and mentions stress only in passing: prefixes and proclitic particles are 'never stressed', and /ɨ/ 'usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables'. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (snippets only, no page number) give a group-level rule for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages: initial stress in disyllables, second-syllable stress occasionally when the first syllable has a central vowel, illustrated with Bagirmi. These two are not in direct contradiction (different word lengths, different scope: language-specific aside vs. group generalization) but do not add up to a single stated rule; both would be consistent with penultimate stress, which no source claims. Tucker 1940 and Sampson 1997 contributed nothing (snippets without a stress remark; not accessible).

sources.note: No stress section and no placement rule. Sec. 3: 'Baka has a two-register tone system' (H/L, lexical + grammatical). Stress only in passing, sec. 2.2 pp. 69-70: /ɨ/ 'occurs in morphemes which are never stressed such as prefixes and proclitic grammatical particles' and 'usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables'; note 5 p. 84: 'it is not impossible that a stress rule.. could be found to handle [ɨ] as a reduced allophone'. Sec. 6: question intonation has extra-high pitch on the penultimate syllables (sentence-level).
